                    ### Question
                    A 55-year-old asthmatic patient goes to the ER with an exacerbation. One hour after the administration of supplemental oxygen and two nebulizations of salbutamol the patient does not improve. On examination, he breathed at 42 rpm with supraclavicular drainage and presented disseminated inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. The peak flow has dropped from 310 to 220 L / min. A gasometry extracted with oxygen at 28% shows a pO2 of 54 mmHg and a pCO2 of 35 mmHg. Which of the following attitudes seems LESS indicated?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Increase oxygen flow.
opb. Administer 80 mg of methylprednisolone iv.
opc. Nebulize ipratropium bromide together with salbutamol every 20 minutes.
opd. Administer intravenous magnesium
ope. Start non-invasive mechanical ventilation.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient is experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation, evidenced by high respiratory rate, wheezing, decreased peak flow, and severe hypoxemia (pO2 of 54 mmHg). Increasing oxygen flow (option opa) is less indicated as it does not address the underlying bronchospasm. Administering 80 mg of methylprednisolone IV (option opb) is appropriate as corticosteroids are crucial in reducing inflammation during severe exacerbations. Nebulizing ipratropium bromide with salbutamol (option opc) is also indicated, as it can help alleviate bronchospasm. Administering intravenous magnesium (option opd) is supported by evidence as it can help in severe exacerbations by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Starting non-invasive mechanical ventilation (option ope) may be necessary due to severe hypoxemia, making it a valid option. Therefore, the least indicated option is to increase oxygen flow, as it does not treat the bronchospasm causing the exacerbation.
